extracted.intended_audience: The Spectator's literate public interested in manners, conversation, and conduct (early-18th-century polite society)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and prescriptive observations for authors of short periodical essays about social conduct, conversation, and public performance (e.g., reading prayers, behaviour in company, treatment of beauty). Focuses on what counts as proper/unbecoming behaviour and how to present it in prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love-letter style: disinterested passion and devotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters should express dis-interested passion, humility, devotion, gratitude and a sense of religious or moral seriousness (examples: 'with what dis-interested Passion, _I am ever Yours_'; closings like 'Your most Obedient, most Devoted Servant').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show sincere affection without vanity; use modest, devotional language and courteous closings. Brief apologies for crude paper or haste are appropriate; concise, heartfelt statements ('I could write a Volume to you, but all the Language on Earth would fail') are preferable to grandiose ostentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not obtrude personal cares in company
rubrics_metrics.description: Cares, Distresses, Diseases, Uneasinesses, and Dislikes of our own, are by no means to be obtruded upon our Friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When among sociable company, avoid recounting personal complaints that force others into 'real or feigned Affliction.' If one laments in company where others are cheerful, one should not be surprised if one is gently directed to retire; personal maladies belong to physicians and private spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain cheerfulness and evenness of mind in conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no real Life, but chearful Life; keep up the cheerfulness of our spirits and never let them sink below an inclination to be well-pleased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursue bodily exercise and an easy mind to preserve evenness; avoid excessive extremes of joy or dejection. Treat laughter and weeping as situationally appropriate, not habitual signs; aim for a sober temper that resists spleen, envy, and impertinent mirth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate a philosophical moderation about life and death
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a temper of mind that views this life modestly and looks to another world to moderate passions: 'Let us be Adventurers for another World' and have but a very mean opinion of this life to enjoy it rightly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A stoic/modest prospect toward worldly success preserves tranquility and makes pleasures less dependent on fortune. This is presented as a practical remedy for melancholy and discontent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware affectation; favor natural simplicity over artifice (especially in beauty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural simplicity of aspect and behaviour is preferable to studied artifice; affectation undermines genuine charms (e.g., 'Amaryllis...extreamly improved with the Arts of Good-Breeding, without leaving Nature' vs. 'Dulcissa...almost a Beauty by Nature, but more than one by Art').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid contrived gestures or studied indifference; training in manners should not substitute for natural grace. The essay illustrates types (Amaryllis, Dulcissa, Merab, etc.) as examples of how artifice, excessive wit, or calculated familiarity can spoil true beauty or virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using beauty as a weapon of deceit or domination
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty may be 'a short liv'd Tyranny' or 'a silent Fraud' capable of imposing without language; it can be used to deceive (Omnamante) or command (Eudosia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers are warned to be alert to those who use appearance to manipulate; moral character should be valued above mere form. The essay gives archetypes — the deceitful charming woman, the commanding noble beauty — to show how beauty combined with vice or ambition is dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not substitute wealth for learning in disputes (avoid wagerers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Young men who 'wager themselves into Statesmen, Historians, Geographers, Mathematicians' by betting to prove points are abusing discourse—using pocket strength to bully ignorance into seeming learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from accepting or making wagers to settle arguments; value genuine knowledge over betting-assertions. If opponents exploit wealth to silence others, the remedy is to discourage that compendious (shortcut) path to wisdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect public conversational space (no excessive whistling or singing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals who whistle or sing opera-tunes 'in a full House' are trespassers on the public room; they have no right to behave as if in an empty room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divide public spaces' auditory 'portion of the room' and prevent those who hear farther than their share from interrupting lawful discourse. Treat noisy interrupters as nuisances equivalent to public trespass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appoint exemplary models to teach proper reading of public prayers
rubrics_metrics.description: To remedy bad reading of the Common Prayer, set a Person of great Ability as a Pattern at public conventions so others (including clergy) can learn by example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exemplary performance (annual assemblies, conventions) as pedagogical tools: Example convinces both the learned and the ignorant; an admired reader's demonstration will teach clarity, strength, manner, and posture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read public prayers with clarity, emphasis, and fervour
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader should 'Read with Clearness, Loudness, and Strength' so that prayer draws attention and devotion; Confession should be read with 'resigned Humility,' Absolution with 'comfortable Authority,' Thanksgivings with 'Religious Joy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid running the service over as mere formality. Place emphasis properly, give the correct accent to words, and vary voice according to the nature of sentences. Reading should move the congregation and elicit the corresponding affections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid uneven 'Pindarick' or spasmodic reading delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Pindarick readers alternate extremes (five or six words deliberate, then five or six words hasty; exalted voice then submissive) producing an uneven, affectated performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for evenness of voice and delivery; do not adopt sudden, capricious tonal shifts that distract or suggest insincerity. The admired reader offers a steady model to cure these affectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain proper posture and demeanour while reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who 'affect a rakish negligent Air by folding their Arms, and lolling on their Book' show indecency; proper reading includes 'comely Erection of Body.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical comportment (posture, attentive bearing) is part of effective public reading and piety. Correct posture supports clarity of delivery and demonstrates reverence for the duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'cant'—sudden exclamations, whining, and unusual tones
rubrics_metrics.description: Cant denotes 'sudden Exclamations, Whinings, unusual Tones, and in fine all Praying and Preaching, like the unlearned'—a pejorative for affected, unintelligible, or whining religious delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish fervour from cant: genuine fervent reading is intelligible and measured, whereas cant is mannered and obscure. Avoid the dialectal, whining, or unintelligible habits associated with 'Andrew Cant' and similar figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not modernize or 'mend' liturgical language carelessly
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers who 'mend the Language as they go on, crying instead of Pardoneth and Absolveth, Pardons and Absolves' corrupt the dignity and sense of liturgical phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve the form and gravity of the language in public worship; avoid casual modernization or flippant substitutions that show indifference or ignorance of the text's solemnity.
